Viscous Burgers 2D/3D · JCP campaign · updated 2026-10-19 05:49 UTC

Does the reduced model's cost depend on bank width, and not on the mesh?

Priorities 1 and 2 are done; priority 3 is half done. Cost does not depend on the mesh in 2D or 3D, and in 2D neither does accuracy; accuracy improves with bank width up to r = 384. But a coarse spectral full solver is faster at equal accuracy (K2 fires in 2D and 3D), and a standard POD reduced model with hyper-reduction beats ours on speed and worst-case error. The paper's case rests on mesh-independent cost and mesh-free evaluation.

The four core questions

Cost vs meshpass2D: 8/8 settings flat from 256² to 4096² (largest max/min 1.016, bar 1.25). 3D: flat from 64³ to 384³ (max/min 1.007–1.091).
Accuracy vs meshpass2D: 8/8 settings give the same error on every mesh, within margin.
Accuracy vs bank widthmonotoneError drops from r=128 to 256 to 384 on every mesh. Going to 512 does not improve.
Cost vs bank widthfailCost does grow with r, but 7 of 8 kernel timings grow more slowly than their operation counts predict.

Against standard reduced models (POD)

H-base fails. A standard POD reduced model with ECSW or Q-DEIM hyper-reduction, tuned on the same validation cases, is both faster and better in the worst case than our model for 8 of 8 settings at 1024², 8 of 8 at 256², and, in 3D, 2 of the 4 fully qualified settings (plus 5 of 5 diagnostic ones). For the other 2 qualified 3D settings neither model dominated, but that result is held back because the 3D POD basis failed its adequacy check.

These are development-cohort, in-sample comparisons, and in some pairs our median error is lower. The 2D tuning budgets are close enough that it is unresolved whether they count as equal; in 3D the POD model got less tuning than ours.

The other "k": head size K

With the nonlinear head (latent size K), cost is still flat in the mesh. At the same online cost, though, the plain linear span with r = 128 is more accurate than the K = 16 head. Too few of the K = 4, 8 and 32 heads passed the solver checks to say how error changes with K.

Against the full simulation (2D)

K2 fires in 2D as well. For every reduced-model setting, the cheapest full solver that is at least as accurate is a spectral solver on a coarse grid (N = 24 or 48). At 4096² the reduced models run at 0.05–0.71× its speed (21 qualified settings). Against a conventional upwind solver, or a central solver on the same 4096² grid, the reduced model is still several times faster, but those are weaker opponents.

This retracts the earlier 13.6× figure as a claim against the best full solver; it only held against a same-mesh upwind solver.

Against the full simulation (3D)

The kill criterion K2 fires: at 384³ a spectral full-order solver reaches the reduced model's accuracy faster. The reduced models run at 0.008–0.16× its speed. Against our own earlier 3D setups the new configurations are 2.0×, 5.4× and 17.2× faster.

Correction: the configurations behind those 2.0–17× speed-ups fail the quadrature check (only 4 of 55 tested 3D settings pass), so they are not yet speed-ups of fully qualified settings. Priority 3 re-times the qualified ones. Per the plan, the paper reports speed plainly and leads with mesh-independence.

Words used here

  • Bank width r: how many basis coefficients the reduced model solves for (the "k" in the question).
  • Mesh: grid points per side of the full simulation (256² up to 4096² in 2D).
  • Full-order / spectral solver: the conventional simulation we compare against; "spectral" uses fast Fourier-type transforms.
  • K2: the plan's pre-registered "we do not beat the best full solver" outcome.
  • BE, CN-R: first- and second-order time stepping.
